meta.title: Who really said "If you want to be a Millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Richard Branson does tell this joke — but not in these words. The wording traces to a 2001 Harvard Business School case epigraph, not to Branson himself.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you want to be a Millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline'?
meta.ogDescription: Branson tells the joke, in his own phrasing. This exact sentence comes from a 2001 Harvard case epigraph — and the joke's formula dates to 1950.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: b. 18 July 1950 · English entrepreneur, founder of Virgin Atlantic and the Virgin Group
answer.sourceLine: Branson really does tell this joke — he told CNBC in 2024, “I personally have said that the best way of becoming a millionaire is to start off as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry.” But that is his wording, not this one: the sentence quoted here surfaces as an unsourced epigraph in a 2001 Harvard Business School case, credited onward to an MSNBC travel article that can no longer be found, and no Branson speech, book or transcript is known to carry it.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Harvard Business School Case No. 801354, by Jody Hoffer Gittell & Charles A. O’Reilly — published 10 February 2001; the copy consulted is stamped REV: OCTOBER 29, 2001
An endnote pointing to P. Greenberg, “Why JetBlue will be different,” MSNBC — an article we could not locate online
CNBC Make It interview, 29 April 2024, which the outlet notes was “edited and condensed for clarity”

source.excerpt:
Where have you heard this before? We’re starting a new low-fare airline. We’re going to offer low-fare tickets and go to the big cities.
— Financial Analyst

If you want to be a millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline.
— Richard Branson, Founder, Virgin Atlantic Airways

Keep an eye on JetBlue. That could prove to be a successful operation.
— Herb Kelleher, Co-founder, CEO, Southwest Airlines
trail: English Wikiquote lists the line among its Richard Branson quotes and traces it to “P. Greenberg, ‘Why JetBlue will be different,’ MSNBC as cited in Gittell and O’Reilly (October, 2001) Harvard Business School Press Reprint No. 9-801-354” — while flagging the entry as still needing a source (Wikiquote ↗).

That case is real: JetBlue Airways: Starting from Scratch by Jody Hoffer Gittell and Charles A. O’Reilly, Harvard Business School Case No. 801354, published 10 February 2001, twenty pages (Harvard Business Publishing ↗). Reading the case text itself confirms the line: it is the second of three epigraphs on page one, credited to “Richard Branson, Founder, Virgin Atlantic Airways,” with an endnote pointing back to the Greenberg MSNBC piece. The MSNBC article could not be found in any web archive we searched.

Branson does use the joke, in his own phrasing. Asked how he prepares for the worst case of a risky bet, he told CNBC Make It: “I personally have said that the best way of becoming a millionaire is to start off as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry” (CNBC, 29 April 2024 ↗). Note the “I personally have said” — a claim to telling it, not to coining it.

The formula is far older than Virgin Atlantic. Quote Investigator traces the joke family — make a small fortune in a risky business by starting with a large one — to a February 1950 Earl Wilson newspaper column, where it was credited to the singer Leo Fuld, and follows it through night clubs, Wall Street, hockey, commodities and wineries (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The case prints “millionaire” in lower case; the version circulating on quote sites capitalises it. Note what the case does not give: no date, no venue, no publication for Branson’s remark — only an endnote to a travel column.

source.rightsNote: No first publication can be fixed for this exact sentence. The oldest source we located is a 2001 Harvard Business School case epigraph, and the article it names as its own source — an MSNBC piece by P. Greenberg — is no longer findable, so it is not possible to say who first put the words in this order. Both documented carriers of the joke are modern and under copyright to their publishers (Harvard Business School Publishing; CNBC); nothing here is public domain.

author.name: Richard Branson
author.heading: About Richard Branson
author.metaLine: b. 18 July 1950 · English entrepreneur · founder of the Virgin Group
author.bio: Richard Branson co-founded Virgin Records in 1972 and took the brand into aviation with Virgin Atlantic, whose maiden flight left London Gatwick for Newark on 22 June 1984. He was knighted in 2000. He has told CNBC that he sold Virgin Records precisely because the airline’s failure would have been the more damaging loss — which is the same anxiety the millionaire-and-billionaire joke is built on, and the reason he tells it against himself.

copyAttribution: Attributed to Richard Branson — but the wording is secondhand. The earliest source found is the epigraph of Harvard Business School case 801354, "JetBlue Airways: Starting from Scratch" (2001), which credits an MSNBC article that can no longer be located. Branson's own version, to CNBC in 2024: "the best way of becoming a millionaire is to start off as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry." The joke's formula is documented from February 1950 onward, applied to many industries.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost
misattribution.intro: The sentence is printed on hundreds of quote sites under Richard Branson’s name with no source at all. Two things disappear in the copying.

items.why: The one version we could verify in Branson’s own voice runs differently: “I personally have said that the best way of becoming a millionaire is to start off as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry” (CNBC, 29 April 2024 ↗, an interview the outlet notes was “edited and condensed for clarity”). The circulating sentence — capital M, “launch a new airline” — is not tied to any recorded occasion.

The formula predates Virgin Atlantic by decades. Quote Investigator dates the earliest instance it found to a February 1950 Earl Wilson newspaper column crediting the singer Leo Fuld, and follows it through night clubs, Wall Street, hockey, commodities and wineries (Quote Investigator ↗). Its airline form still circulates unattributed as “an old joke about airlines” (The Motley Fool, 2008 ↗).

The Harvard case never claims to have heard Branson say it — its endnote passes the line on from a travel article by P. Greenberg, “Why JetBlue will be different,” on MSNBC, which we could not locate anywhere online. Wikiquote reproduces exactly that chain and still marks the entry as needing a source (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Branson genuinely tells this joke and has said so himself — “I personally have said that the best way of becoming a millionaire is to start off as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry” (CNBC, 29 April 2024 ↗). He simply did not invent it, and he is not documented anywhere saying it in the words the internet hands him.

context.heading: Why the joke keeps getting told
lead: The line lands because the arithmetic behind it is real. Aviation runs on enormous fixed costs, thin margins and violent cycles, and the industry’s own folklore has said so for a long time without anyone’s name attached: “How do you make a small fortune in the airlines? Start with a large fortune!” is quoted simply as “an old joke about airlines” (The Motley Fool, 14 January 2008 ↗).

Branson had the standing to tell it against himself. Virgin Atlantic’s maiden flight went from London Gatwick to Newark on 22 June 1984 (Wikipedia ↗), and in the CNBC interview he explains what the joke actually meant for him in practice: he hedged, negotiating the right to hand Virgin’s first plane back to Boeing at the end of the first year, so the worst case was roughly a year’s profits from Virgin Records (CNBC, 29 April 2024 ↗).
context.detailsSummary: What the Harvard case was actually doing with the line
detailsBody: The 2001 case is about JetBlue, not Virgin. Gittell and O’Reilly open it with three voices — a sceptical financial analyst (“Where have you heard this before? We’re starting a new low-fare airline”), the Branson joke, and Herb Kelleher of Southwest saying “Keep an eye on JetBlue. That could prove to be a successful operation.” The point of the trio is to set the odds against a new low-fare carrier.

Branson’s sentence is used there as received industry wisdom, not as a documented utterance — which is exactly how it has travelled ever since. Quote sites lifted the epigraph, dropped the endnote, and capitalised the M.
context.pull: The earliest version of the joke on record predates Branson’s own birth.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Richard Branson page lists 'If you want to be a Millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline.' in its Quotes section, citing 'P. Greenberg, "Why JetBlue will be different," MSNBC as cited in Gittell and O'Reilly (October, 2001) Harvard Business School Press Reprint No. 9-801-354', with a {{source}} flag marking the citation as insufficient.

The HBS case 'JetBlue Airways: Starting from Scratch' (9-801-354, REV: OCTOBER 29, 2001, by Jody Hoffer Gittell and Charles O'Reilly) opens with three epigraphs; the second reads 'If you want to be a millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline. — Richard Branson, Founder, Virgin Atlantic Airways' with superscript endnote 2, whose endnote reads 'Ibid.' referring to endnote 1: 'P. Greenberg, "Why JetBlue will be different," MSNBC.' The first epigraph is credited to a Financial Analyst and the third to Herb Kelleher.
Harvard Business Publishing lists 'JetBlue Airways: Starting from Scratch' by Jody Hoffer Gittell and Charles A. O'Reilly, product number 801354, publication date 10 February 2001, 20 pages.

CNBC (Tom Huddleston Jr., published 29 April 2024) quotes Richard Branson saying: 'I had an instinct that if we created the best-quality airline flying across the Atlantic, it would survive. I knew it was very risky. I personally have said that the best way of becoming a millionaire is to start off as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry. So in case my instinct was wrong, I negotiated the right to hand [Virgin's first plane] back to Boeing at the end of the first year.' The article states the interview was edited and condensed for clarity, and that selling Virgin Records protected the airline.

Quote Investigator traces the 'make a small fortune by starting with a large fortune' joke family to a February 1950 Earl Wilson syndicated column crediting singer Leo Fuld, and documents later versions applied to night clubs, Wall Street, hockey, commodities and wineries. The article does not cover airlines, aviation or Richard Branson.

The Motley Fool (Chuck Saletta, 14 January 2008) opens with 'Q: How do you make a small fortune in the airlines? A: Start with a large fortune!' and introduces it as 'an old joke about airlines' without crediting anyone.
Wikipedia states Virgin Atlantic was founded in 1984 and its maiden flight from London–Gatwick to Newark took place on 22 June 1984.
Wikipedia gives Richard Branson's date of birth as 18 July 1950, states he co-founded Virgin Records in 1972, established Virgin Atlantic in 1984, and was knighted in 2000.
